body.text: Why does Scam center still shape capital allocation and market pricing across global desks? Behind the headline numbers lies a structural mechanism that quietly governs liquidity, risk, and long-term purchasing power.

A scam centre or scam center (also called a scam compound, fraud factory or fraud park) is an organised workplace in which groups of people commit remote fraud on an industrial scale, usually by telephone, messaging apps, social media and fake investment or trading websites.

The term is most often applied to the fortified compounds run by Chinese-speaking criminal syndicates in Myanmar, Cambodia, Laos and the Philippines, where many of the workers are themselves victims of human trafficking held in conditions of modern slavery.

Operations built on the same commercial logic but without trafficked labour, staffed mainly by local employees paid salaries and commissions, have run for more than a decade in post-Soviet Eurasia, above all in Ukraine and Georgia, as well as in Israel, Cyprus and the western Balkans.

body.text: Comparable centres operate in South Asia, West Africa, the Gulf and Latin America.

Reliable figures are hard to establish, and the available estimates differ in scope and method. In 2026 the UN human rights office cited estimates that at least 300,000 people were working in scam operations in Southeast Asia alone, and by late 2025 trafficking victims of nearly 80 nationalities had been identified in scam centres.

The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC) put the annual take of scam centres worldwide at about US$1 trillion in March 2026, roughly 1% of global GDP, and in Cambodia, Laos and Myanmar scam revenue has been estimated to equal a large share of formal GDP.
Investigations in several regions have found scam centres organised as businesses, although the degree of coercion varies.

Many buy contact data from marketing affiliates, divide staff into departments with team leaders and sales targets, train recruits on written scripts, track victims in customer relationship management software and reward the best performers with commissions, bonuses and parties, while relying on payment processors, money mules and cryptocurrency services to move the proceeds.

Criminal and corruption cases in 2025 and 2026 reached Chen Zhi, the founder of Cambodia's Prince Group and an adviser to the prime minister, Kok An, a Cambodian senator, Grigol Liluashvili, the former head of Georgia's State Security Service, whom a Georgian court sentenced to 13 years in prison in September 2026, and officials of Ukraine's Prosecutor General's Office.

Several large crackdowns have followed pressure from the countries whose citizens are defrauded or trafficked, including China, the United States, the United Kingdom, South Korea and EU Member States, but researchers report that operations tend to move elsewhere or continue covertly rather than shut down.
Terminology

The English term "fraud factory" was in use by 2022, when it appeared in the headline of a report in The Sydney Morning Herald. Chinese-language media call the compounds "fraud parks" (诈骗园区, zhàpiàn yuánqū), often shortened to "parks" (园区).
In Ukraine and Russia the operations are usually called "call centres", and Ukrainian workers refer to the workplace simply as the office.

Employees of European investment-fraud call centres speak of the people they defraud as clients or depositors, while workers in Southeast Asian compounds describe their targets as pigs to be fattened with trust before the slaughter, which gave the pig butchering scam its name.
The high-pressure telephone sale of worthless securities from shared offices, an older and related form of fraud, is known as a boiler room.
Types
Scam centres fall into two broad models, which differ above all in how they obtain and treat their workers.

GI-TOC nevertheless treats them as parts of one global industry, since reports from different regions describe the same commercial methods: acquiring potential victims at scale, taking them through scripted stages, measuring staff against targets, relying on laundering networks and depending on protection by officials.
Forced-labour compounds

In the forced-labour model, associated above all with Myanmar, Cambodia, Laos and the Philippines, criminal syndicates hold workers in walled compounds, casinos and hotel complexes, usually in border areas and special economic zones. Many of the workers have been recruited with false job offers, trafficked across borders and stripped of their passports.
Compounds using trafficked workers have also been documented in the United Arab Emirates, and the model has since spread to other regions (see § Globalisation).
Voluntary call centres

In the voluntary model, which predominates in Ukraine, Georgia, the Balkans and Israel, call centres operate from ordinary offices in towns and cities and employ local people who choose the work and are paid salaries and commissions. They specialise in investment fraud and in impersonating banks and the police.
Overlap between the models

The distinction is not absolute. Interpol has stated that not everyone committing fraud in a scam centre is a victim of trafficking, and some workers arrive in Southeast Asian compounds knowing the nature of the work, while some networks in the voluntary model threaten or use violence against staff who want to leave.

In both models the targets have also shifted over time. Ukrainian centres, which began by defrauding Russians, turned to wealthier victims in Europe and North America, and Chinese syndicates in Southeast Asia, whose early victims were mostly Chinese citizens, turned to people elsewhere as Chinese crackdowns intensified. History
Precursors

Organised telephone fraud from shared offices long predates the modern scam centre and developed in several separate strands. The oldest was Taiwanese and Chinese: Ivan Franceschini, Ling Li and Mark Bo, the authors of the first comprehensive account of the Southeast Asian scam industry, trace its origins to Taiwan in the 1990s.

The syndicates behind Asian romance and investment scams grew out of the offshore gambling industry that emerged from China in the early 2000s, and a 2009 crime-fighting agreement between Taiwan and China, which led to more than 1,600 arrests of fraud suspects by 2011, pushed many Taiwanese groups to relocate to Southeast Asia.

The second strand was Israeli: over the decade to 2017, an industry selling binary options, forex and contracts for difference to small investors abroad brought in up to US$10 billion a year, according to The Times of Israel.

Many firms operated without any regulation, while others obtained licences from the Cyprus Securities and Exchange Commission that allowed them to sell throughout the European Union. After a series of investigative reports, the Knesset unanimously banned the binary options industry in October 2017, and the ban took effect on 26 January 2018.

By then many call centres had already moved to Ukraine and elsewhere in Eastern Europe, and former employees reported that companies had relocated to Cyprus, Kyiv, Georgia and Belgrade. Some operators simply switched to fraudulent forex, contract-for-difference and cryptocurrency products.
Another strand developed in India, where call centres defrauded people in the United States.

In 2016 the US Department of Justice charged 61 individuals and entities, among them five call centres in Ahmedabad whose staff posed as officials of the Internal Revenue Service and US Citizenship and Immigration Services, the frauds had claimed tens of thousands of victims and caused losses of hundreds of millions of dollars.
Post-Soviet Eurasia since 2014

In Russia, telephone fraud had long been organised from inside the penal system (see § Russia). According to GI-TOC, Ukraine's scam call-centre industry emerged in 2014, when Russia annexed Crimea and invaded eastern Ukraine.

The war ended cooperation between Russian and Ukrainian law enforcement, which made it far less risky for call centres on one side of the front line to defraud people on the other. Early Ukrainian operations mostly targeted Russian citizens, and only later turned to Ukrainians and other Europeans as well.

Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022 was followed by a rise in fraud: the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) recorded that fraud cases in Ukraine more than tripled in 2023 compared with 2021 and 2022, and estimated that about 1,500 call centres were operating across the country.

Similar operations spread across the region. A 2026 GI-TOC assessment identified Ukraine, Russia and Georgia as the main hotspots and found that Armenia, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, although less active, were catching up.
